justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift assumption from a baseline near 417.89. At the one-day horizon, I essentially anchored to the last known price with near-zero expected movement, since equity index prices over a single trading session have an expected return very close to zero when no specific catalyst is imminent. At the one-week horizon, I nudged the estimate slightly higher to about 418.50, reflecting the small positive drift embedded in long-run equity returns but keeping the adjustment minimal given the short window. At the one-month horizon, I moved to roughly 420, again reflecting that same modest positive drift assumption scaled to approximately four weeks, consistent with historical average monthly returns on broad equity indices in the low single-digit annualized range.

The confidence interval widths were driven primarily by realized volatility scaling with the square root of time. At one day, I collapsed the interval to the point estimate itself, which in retrospect was overly aggressive and reflects an assumption of near-certain price discovery that is not really defensible — even intraday, prices can move one to two percent. At one week, I used a rough annualized volatility assumption of around 15–18 percent for a broad index, which translates to a weekly standard deviation of roughly 1.5–2 percent, giving a 90 percent interval of about plus or minus 5–6 percent. At one month, I widened further to roughly plus or minus 12 percent around the point estimate, consistent with that same volatility assumption scaled to a monthly horizon.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside these intervals include a sudden shift in Federal Reserve policy signaling, a meaningful deterioration in corporate earnings guidance, or a geopolitical shock such as an escalation in an ongoing conflict. On the upside, a surprise positive resolution to trade tensions, stronger-than-expected economic data, or a dovish pivot in central bank communication could drive prices well above the upper bound of my one-month interval. Liquidity events or technical breakdowns in market structure, though rare, represent fat-tail risks that my normally-distributed framework does not fully capture.

It is also worth acknowledging that my one-day interval was essentially a degenerate forecast and should not be interpreted as genuine confidence. A more honest one-day 90 percent interval would span at least one to two percent in either direction, reflecting normal daily price fluctuation. This is a calibration shortcoming I would correct in future forecasts by always maintaining a minimum interval width proportional to at least one day of typical realized volatility.
